As one of the first members of the State Anti-Tuberculosis Commission, Mr. Ashcraft undertook perhaps his greatest humanitarian work, and continued it until his death.

The last decade of his life was a battle with ill health, and the drafts on his diminishing strength were met with an earnest philosophy that gained increased admiration at the end the assertion that "No knight of old, however stalwart, ever bore a more laundless[?] shield." He is credited with the attainment of personal self-mastery a gentler or more chivalrous soul.

When this announcement of his death was made, on February 9, 1920, it was written of him, "He was imbued to an extraordinary degree with that quality which drew all to him toward the end, knew how closely he must have knit himself as a teacher and friend—he was some how always 'Father-Friend.' The words bring up the sweet face that lives in every line of his life, a face that was alive yet always the same kind, self-sacrificing sition[?], contributing of both mental and moral to every worthy cause."

To Mr. and Mrs. Ashcraft were born ten children, three of whom died in infancy, thus leaving eight to tell life the child. The surviving seven are:

Mary Ellis, an A. B. graduate of Judson College in Marion, Alabama, who married Henry Duncan Moore, Major of Engineers in the United States Army, and later was Superintendent of the Midwest Refining Company of the Salt Creek Field of Wyoming.

Cyrus Andrew, a student of Auburn and the University of Michigan, who was at one time a Vice-President of the United States Steel Corporation.

Martha Ellis, who was a student of Florence State Teachers College, and of other schools.

Estelle Hurt, who is an A. B. graduate of Judson College and also attended the Library School of the University of Wisconsin;
